synopsis: Operator behavior can change positively or negatively after protective technology is introduced; automatic braking may prompt reliance, resistance, overrides or disabling after nuisance interventions [f791, f1982]. Mining evidence strongly establishes that operators override or disable functions that interfere with production, although frequency across sites is unknown; the June 2017 fatal continuous-miner investigation found emergency-stop override had become common practice [f3449, f3294]. Off-road risk compensation remains a credible but unmeasured hypothesis: worker reports describe riskier positioning and a false sense of security, but representative surface-mining evidence of faster driving, closer following or greater risk-taking was not found [f3424, f3034, f3455]. Warning-only fleet data cannot reliably characterize future automatic-braking behavior because operator reactions censor logs and behavior changes when warnings become interventions; shadow mode also cannot establish whether operators counteract actual braking [f7940, f7480, f8205, f598]. Long-term adaptation cannot be established through simulators or the four-month validation window, so the booklet recommends explicit behavioral validation, staged release with field monitoring, and collection of missing quantitative data during pilot deployment [f580, f378, f1105, f11859, f11860].
